newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - April 24.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - April 24.

text.p: Hongkong and Shanghai Bank launched a HK$2.0 billion floating rate certificate of deposit issue on Wednesday, its second big deal this year.
The three-year certificates were priced at par to float at 22 basis points over the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate. With fees, the all-in return is 27 basis points to top-tier managers.
Bankers pronounced the pricing tight, but nevertheless predicted the issue would attract a decent response because of the quality of the issuer.
"The pricing is very, very low but it's Hongkong Bank so people are sure to want to participate for relationship reasons," said a syndicate manager at a European bank.
Top-rated Hongkong Bank has a local currency rating of A2 from Moody's Investors Service. It is one of three Hong Kong note issuing banks.
Hongkong Bank is a regular issuer in the debt market. In addition to its HK$3.5 billion five-year issue set in January, it frequently places paper privately.
The five-year FRCD issue launched in January paid an all-in return of 38 basis points. It attracted many lenders and was increased to HK$3.5 billion from HK$2.0 billion in syndication.
A number of banks are expected to raise Hong Kong dollar funding over the next month or so, adding their names to the list of banks already in the market.
Bank of East Asia and Union Bank of Hong Kong have FRCDs in syndication now.
The HK$1.2 billion three-year FRCD for Wing Hang Bank will be launched later this week, and Hongkong Chinese Bank also is on the outlook.

Bankers also expect the HK$1.0 billion FRCD for Malaysia's Public Bank to be launched shortly. That deal is expected to attract a strong response because of the rarity of Malaysian issues in general and of Malaysian Hong Kong dollar issues in particular.
Bankers attributed the wealth of new Hong Kong dollar issues to a number of factors.
They said many Hong Kong banks are refinancing as outstanding issues mature. Some banks also are building their books in anticipation of funding the many infrastructure projects in Hong Kong.
The handover to China also is a factor, some sources said.
"The banks are all very liquid, they are not in a hurry to get the money, but they want all the commitments lined up in case anything goes wrong at the handover," said the syndicate manager.

"Nobody has any fears because they know deep down nothing can go wrong because they know the PRC will assure that everything is smooth, but they want to be sure that they are not the last ones looking for money," the manager added.

Other bankers said borrowers are rushing to finish up business before the handover for another reason -- so many holidays have been mandated to celebrate the event that markets will be effectively closed for several days in late June and early July.
Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
